notes.body: The scholar diagnoses the outside and inside of religion like a doctor. Inner meaning with no outer practice is a spirit with no body — a wraith that can't walk the earth or move a stone. Outer ritual with no inner meaning is a body with no spirit — a corpse whose limbs you move through the motions, but which doesn't live. Practice without meaning is dead; meaning without practice is a ghost; the two only subsist through each other.

Salt sea water is the outer, exoteric knowledge — vast, it covers the whole earth and preserves things from rotting, but you can't drink it and nothing grows from it. Fresh spring water is the inner, esoteric knowledge — the only water that feeds the field. Water the crops with the sea and you scorch the earth; you need the sweet water the summoners carry to actually grow a living soul.
notes.anchor: salt sea vs fresh spring water

notes.body: Everything in the cosmos comes in a pair — heaven and earth, sun and moon, salt water and sweet — and because each has a peer it can point down to a rank below it. Air is the one exception: unpaired, it mixes with everything and is encompassed by nothing. Set the earth against air and it's a seal ring dropped on an endless plain; set the whole heaven against air and it's an egg on that plain. Having no peer, air can only point upward — to the One who has no like.

The boy catches an apparent contradiction: one verse forbids striking likenesses for God, another says the highest likeness belongs to Him. The scholar untangles it by distinguishing two kinds of sign. A lesser sign is forbidden because it slots God into a list alongside His creatures, like saying a river points to a guide. The highest likeness is licensed precisely because air has no equal in creation — so it can't demote Him to just another rung. It's the sign that announces the failure of signs: in the very act of pointing up, it declares it can't capture what it points to.
notes.anchor: why the highest likeness is allowed
